clue.text: Row about newspaper backing Panama?

indicators.note: Something placed about a thing is wrapped round it, so the row closes over the letters that follow.

parts.note: a row of seats in a stand is a tier

indicators.note: A newspaper's backing is its support in the surface; as an instruction it asks for those two letters read from the back.

parts.note: the Financial Times, Britain's pink business paper, signs itself FT

explanation.surface: A quarrel about a paper coming out in favour of Panama.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' is the line of seats, not the argument the surface wants, and Panama is a hat: a titfer is Cockney rhyming slang, from tit for tat.
explanation.definitionFit: A Panama is one particular straw hat and a titfer is slang for any hat, so the definition works by naming an example.

clue.text: From Goethe, a tremendous play enacted here

indicators.note: Saying the answer comes from these words points at the words themselves, and the letters are already sitting in them in order.

parts.note: the letters run on unbroken across the comma and the two spaces

explanation.surface: A grand production of Goethe, played with enormous energy.
explanation.walkthrough: German drama in the surface and an English word underneath it: the run starts in the middle of Goethe's name, which is where nobody looks first.
explanation.definitionFit: A theatre is the building a play is performed in, so the definition names it by what happens inside rather than by any synonym.

clue.text: I then took odds on twenty in order to get hitched

indicators.note: put in order, so the jumbled letters are arranged properly
odds on a word means its odd-numbered letters, first, third and fifth, of the word twenty

parts.note: its odd letters are used

explanation.surface: Someone who placed a bet at twenty-to-one and then arranged to marry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'odds on twenty' gives TET; add I THEN and TOOK, and 'in order' arranges the whole pool into the answer. 'odds on' reads as betting talk, not letter selection.
explanation.definitionFit: Tying the knot is an idiom for marrying, and getting hitched is a casual way to say the same.

clue.text: One chooses shock treatment in role reversal

definitions.note: The definition is a clause where the answer is a noun: read it as 'one who chooses', a shorthand setters allow themselves because the surface needs a sentence.

indicators.note: Treatment given in something happens inside it, so these letters land within the word beside them rather than next to it.
A reversal turns a thing back to front, and what gets read from its last letter to its first here is the role.

parts.note: the word as it stands, waiting to be turned round
electroconvulsive therapy, the psychiatric treatment that passes a current through the brain, is written ECT

explanation.surface: Somebody volunteering for electric shock therapy when the roles get swapped round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Role reversal' is one idea in the surface and a pair of instructions underneath it, and ECT is a genuine medical abbreviation rather than a crossword invention.
explanation.definitionFit: An elector is one who chooses in the narrow sense of casting a vote, so the word covers anybody entitled to choose at an election.

clue.text: Silly positions must be rejected — I would

indicators.note: Something rejected is thrown back, and a word thrown back is read from its last letter to its first.

parts.note: to position something is to put it somewhere, so the verb matches in the third person
I would shortens to I'd in speech, and the apostrophe goes

explanation.surface: Someone agreeing that ridiculous stances ought to be thrown out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Positions' reads as opinions or postures in the surface and is a plain verb in the wordplay, and the dash covers the switch to a speaker.
explanation.definitionFit: Stupid answers to silly in the sense of lacking sense, not the softer silly of a silly hat or a silly mistake.

clue.text: See 2
Palestine suffering sanctions

indicators.note: A country suffering is in a bad way, and letters in a bad way have come out of the arrangement they were given.

parts.note: all nine letters of the name, rebuilt into a different word

explanation.surface: A news headline about a territory living under imposed sanctions.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder and the definition sit side by side with a single word between them, and the headline reads so naturally that the signal to shuffle disappears into it.
explanation.definitionFit: A sanction in the political sense is a punishment imposed from outside, and penalties are exactly that — punishments handed down.

clue.text: Want to start eating potato

parts.note: to want something is to desire it

indicators.note: The start of a word is the letter it opens with, and only that one letter joins what has gone before.

parts.note: the first letter of the word, taken off the front and nothing else with it

explanation.surface: Somebody too impatient to wait for the meal to begin.
explanation.walkthrough: Desiree is a red-skinned potato variety sold in every British greengrocer, which is how 'potato' can define what looks like a woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Desiree is a named variety of potato, so 'potato' defines by category: the answer is one particular kind of the thing named.

clue.text: Disparate motel with a twist in the tail? End of story!

indicators.text: with a twist in the tail
indicators.note: the end of the word motel is twisted round, its last two letters changing places
the end of a word is its final letter, so only the closing letter of story is used

parts.note: its final letter is taken

explanation.surface: A mixed-up motel story capped with a surprise ending, then the words that close a tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with a twist in the tail' swaps the final two letters of MOTEL to give MOTLE; the last letter of story finishes it.
explanation.definitionFit: A motley collection is varied and ill-assorted, so disparate in its parts.

clue.text: Exploit flyer with imperfect tenses to get personal benefit

parts.note: a feat is an exploit, a daring deed
a heron is a bird, a flyer

indicators.note: imperfect letters are flawed, so the word tenses is rearranged

explanation.surface: A grammar lesson on taking advantage of a bird by using the imperfect tense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'imperfect' looks like grammar beside 'tenses' but it is the anagram signal, making ESNEST.
explanation.definitionFit: Feathering one's nest is an idiom for enriching oneself, often improperly, through one's position.

clue.text: Bowler may be here to give evidence

parts.note: the small word that says where somebody is
a Test is an international cricket match played over five days, the level a top bowler works at

explanation.surface: A man in a bowler hat turning up at court as a witness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bowler' is the hat the surface has you picturing in a courtroom and the cricketer the wordplay wants, and 'here' is a whole word doing the work of two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To attest is to bear witness formally, which is what a witness does in the box: give evidence on oath.

clue.text: Proprietor with joiner in funny comeback

indicators.note: A joiner slotted in goes inside, so the word beside it opens up and takes those letters within it.
A comeback is a return along the way you came, so those letters are read from their far end back to their start.

parts.note: droll is funny in the dry, understated way
the conjunction that joins two clauses together

explanation.surface: A proprietor and a carpenter swapping witty retorts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joiner' is the carpenter in the surface and the grammarian's word in the wordplay — a conjunction joins two clauses, and AND is the plainest one there is.
explanation.definitionFit: A landlord is the proprietor of a pub or of property let to tenants, so 'proprietor' is the general word for what he owns and runs.

clue.text: Nightcap on vacation during jovial preparatory celebration

indicators.note: A word on vacation has been emptied out, so only the letters at its two ends are left standing.

parts.note: a hearty welcome is a jovial one

indicators.note: Something that happens during an event happens inside it, so these letters sit within the word beside them.

parts.note: the two ends of the word, with everything between them gone

explanation.surface: A last drink before bed, taken in the middle of a cheerful party.
explanation.walkthrough: A hen party is the bride's night out before a British wedding, and 'nightcap' does two jobs: the drink in the surface, and a word to be hollowed out.
explanation.definitionFit: A hen party is the celebration held for a bride before her wedding, so 'preparatory' points at what it comes before rather than at anything it prepares.

clue.text: Fill up ten forms, that's more than enough

indicators.note: Forms is the verb here: the letters beside it are made to form something, which they can only do by moving.

parts.note: nine letters, the little words counted in

explanation.surface: Being handed ten forms to complete and deciding that is quite enough bureaucracy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fill up' looks like the instruction printed on the paperwork and 'forms' looks like the paperwork itself; the two swap jobs, one becoming fodder and the other the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Plentiful means present in more than sufficient quantity, so 'more than enough' catches the sense exactly: abundance rather than mere sufficiency.

clue.text: John is one outwardly for hire

indicators.note: What is outward is on the outside, so the phrase this points at wraps round the letter named before it.

parts.note: TO LET is what the sign says on a British property offered for hire
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A man named John who looks, from the outside, as though he can be hired.
explanation.walkthrough: John is American slang for the lavatory, which is why the clue can open with what reads as somebody's first name and still be a definition.
explanation.definitionFit: John is the American colloquial word for a lavatory, so the definition is slang for the answer, dressed up as a man's name.

clue.text: First couple of letters dispatched, so not here

parts.note: the opening pair taken from the alphabet itself, in the order they come
a parcel dispatched has been sent

explanation.surface: A note explaining that the first of the post has already gone out.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters wanted belong to no word in the clue but to the alphabet, which is why picking initials out of the clue itself gets you nowhere.
explanation.definitionFit: Absent means not present, and 'not here' says the same the short way — the state of somebody who has failed to turn up.

clue.text: Relative souper?

parts.note: the soup itself, of the thin clear kind
the ending that turns a thing into the person who deals in it, as a bake becomes a baker

explanation.surface: A relation described, oddly, as a maker of soup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Souper' is not a word, and the question mark admits it: the setter has coined an agent noun for somebody who makes soup, then spelled it a different way.
explanation.definitionFit: A brother is a male sibling, so 'relative' defines by the wider family category the answer belongs to.

clue.text: Prepared letters of support

indicators.note: Preparing something means working it into a new state, and letters worked over like that do not come out as they went in.

parts.note: the seven letters of the word itself, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A bundle of carefully prepared references vouching for somebody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letters of support' is a real phrase, which is what makes it hard to see that 'support' has been cut off the end of it and set to work as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A trestle is the braced frame a table top rests on, so 'support' names the answer by function: the thing that holds another thing up.

clue.text: Sounds like Bath perhaps being in short supply

indicators.note: This asks for the noise the words make rather than their spelling, so what gets written down is not what was handed over.
Perhaps flags an example rather than a synonym: the place named is one of the kind wanted, not the kind itself.

parts.note: Bath, in south-west England, is built on hot springs and gave its name to bathing, so it is one city among the spa towns

explanation.surface: A remark that Bath, of all places, is running short of something.
explanation.walkthrough: In a British accent the R at the join is not sounded, so two words run together into one, and a city on the map turns into a shortage.
explanation.definitionFit: Sparsity is the noun for how thinly something is spread, so whatever is in short supply is present only sparsely.

clue.text: First and last to arrive can generate conflict

indicators.note: The last of a word is the letter it ends on, and only that one is taken from what follows.
What a thing can generate is something new made out of it, and a new word is made out of old letters by moving them.

parts.note: the whole word, all five letters, not the initial of anything
the letter this word ends on

explanation.surface: Whoever turns up first and whoever turns up last making trouble between them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First and last' looks like one instruction to take two letters, and only the second half of it is one: 'first' is five letters of fodder just as it is written.
explanation.definitionFit: Strife is open conflict between people — quarrelling and fighting rather than a mere difference of opinion — which is the sense 'conflict' carries here.

clue.text: Embarrassed to display university degree in an outhouse

indicators.note: A degree hung in a place sits inside it, so these two letters go within the words beside them.

parts.note: an outhouse is a shed, and the article in front supplies the A
a Bachelor of Arts is a BA

explanation.surface: Somebody too shy to hang their degree certificate anywhere but the garden shed.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface frames a certificate and hides it in an outhouse, and 'an' is not scenery: the A in front of the shed is a letter the answer needs.
explanation.definitionFit: Abashed means embarrassed in the particular sense of being shamed out of your confidence, which is the reading 'embarrassed' takes here.

clue.text: Cute name that is for a youngster

parts.note: twee is cute to the point of being sickly
N is the standard abbreviation for name
i.e. is the Latin id est, meaning that is

explanation.surface: A sweet little name given to a small child.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That is' is an everyday phrase in the surface and the abbreviation i.e. in the wordplay, which is the join a solver looks straight past.
explanation.definitionFit: A tweenie is a child between infancy and the teens, roughly eight to twelve, so 'a youngster' names the answer by the age group it covers.

clue.text: Settle where stated in Oxford or Derby

definitions.note: An Oxford and a Derby are each one style of shoe while the answer is a collective noun covering the lot, so the setter is defining by example without the usual question mark.

parts.note: to foot the bill is to settle it

indicators.note: Stated means said out loud, so the word before it is written down as it sounds rather than as the clue spells it.

parts.note: said aloud the two are one noise, and only the spelling changes

explanation.surface: An instruction to pay the bill in the town named — Oxford, or else Derby.
explanation.walkthrough: Oxford and Derby are lace-up shoe styles as well as English cities, and the surface keeps them looking like two places on a map.
explanation.definitionFit: An Oxford and a Derby are two styles of lace-up shoe, so the definition points at the answer by giving a pair of examples of it.

clue.text: Learnt to play the horn

indicators.note: To play with a thing is to knock it about, and letters knocked about will not stay in the order they were given.

parts.note: six letters, exactly the six the answer needs

explanation.surface: Somebody who has taught themselves to play the French horn.
explanation.walkthrough: The horn is not the one the surface plays but the one a stag carries, and 'learnt to play' reads as a single achievement rather than as fodder plus a signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An antler is the branched horn of a deer, so 'horn' defines by the general kind — headgear on a stag rather than anything you blow.

clue.text: Finally enrol in crash diet mañana, got that, but not tomorrow

definitions.text: mañana, got that, but not tomorrow

indicators.note: the letter goes inside the jumbled word
a crash diet, but here crash means the letters of diet are smashed and rearranged
finally means at the very end, so only the closing letter of enrol is used

parts.note: its final letter is taken

explanation.surface: Someone resolving to start a crash diet, but in Spanish fashion, not until tomorrow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crash diet' reads as a whole phrase, but 'crash' rearranges DIET around L. Mañana is Spanish for tomorrow and carries the mark over its n; the English word tomorrow does not.
explanation.definitionFit: The tilde is the wavy accent over the n in mañana, absent from the English equivalent.

clue.text: Best in everything for big Brits

definitions.meaning: the idiom for the choicest of what a country has to offer — you live off it
read literally instead of as an idiom: heavy people, and the country they live in

explanation.surface: A headline claiming that heavier Britons are doing better than everybody else.
explanation.walkthrough: Both readings turn on 'fat': in the idiom it is the richest part of what a country produces, and in the joke it is the people.
explanation.definitionFit: Living off the fat of the land is having the best of everything a place offers; read literally, the fat of Britain is its heavier inhabitants.

clue.text: Ease with which judge accepts falsehood

indicators.note: A judge who accepts something takes it in, so the word before opens up and the next one goes inside it.

parts.note: a referee judges a match, and shortens to REF
a falsehood told on purpose is a lie

explanation.surface: A judge in court quietly letting an untruth go by.
explanation.walkthrough: The judge is not a courtroom one: a referee is the official who judges a game, and 'ease' is a noun here rather than the verb it looks like.
explanation.definitionFit: Relief is the ease that arrives when something unpleasant stops — the noun for that lifting of strain, not comfort in general.

clue.text: Stick poster, but not over there!

parts.note: a poster is an advertisement, AD for short
the opposite of over there is right here

explanation.surface: An instruction to put the poster up on this wall and not on that one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick' is the verb meaning to glue rather than a stick of wood, and the exclamation mark makes the whole thing sound like somebody pointing at a wall.
explanation.definitionFit: To adhere is to stick fast to a surface — glue's sense of the word, though the answer covers sticking to a rule as well.
